items.title: UNICEF raises alarm over 624,000 out-of-school children
items.description: By Musa Ubandawaki, Sokoto The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) has raised concerns over the high number of out-of-school children in Sokoto, Kebbi and Zamfara states, disclosing that about 624,000 children have been identified as being outside the classroom across the three states. The organisation said although about 68,000 children had benefited from interventions to return them to school, the scale of the challenge required urgent government action, increased investment and stronger community mobilisation. UNICEF’s Chief of Field Office in Sokoto, Dr Michael Juma, made this known at a media briefing organised by the organisation’s Sokoto Field Office as part of activities marking the 2026 World Children’s Day. He called for coordinated action by governments, media organisations, traditional institutions, religious leaders and community stakeholders to address challenges confronting children in the region. Juma urged journalists across the three states to intensify public enlightenment, investigative reporting and advocacy to promote children’s rights, strengthen government accountability and ensure access to education, healthcare, nutrition and other essential services. Describing the media as a critical partner in advancing children’s rights, he said journalists must go beyond reporting events to exposing gaps in service delivery and holding relevant authorities accountable. “The media are important duty-bearers in advancing children’s rights. Journalists must provide balanced coverage that highlights development achievements while drawing attention to persistent gaps affecting the wellbeing of children,” he said. He reaffirmed UNICEF’s commitment to strengthening collaboration with the governments of Sokoto, Kebbi and Zamfara, development partners, traditional and religious leaders, and grassroots organisations to guarantee children access to quality and inclusive education, healthcare, adequate nutrition, safe drinking water and social protection. Providing an account of interventions undertaken through UNICEF’s partnerships with the three state governments, Juma disclosed that approximately 98,000 children had benefited from the Teaching at the Right Level (TaRL) programme, designed to improve foundational literacy and numeracy. He said the organisation was also supporting teacher professional development, provision of instructional materials, accelerated basic education, integrated Qur’anic education and innovative learning opportunities, including radio-based education and the Nigeria Learning Passport. According to him, the interventions are particularly targeted at children affected by insecurity, displacement and other emergencies. On healthcare and immunisation, Juma disclosed that approximately 7.8 million children across the three states had been reached through measles-rubella vaccination, while more than five million children were vaccinated during the last concluded polio immunisation campaign. He further said Kebbi State had recorded progress in malaria vaccination, with approximately 148,000 children receiving the first dose and 130,000 receiving the second dose. He stressed that effective healthcare delivery and sustained immunisation campaigns remained essential to reducing preventable childhood deaths and improving children’s survival. On malnutrition, the UNICEF official commended the Sokoto and Zamfara State Governments for committing approximately N100 million and N500 million respectively towards the procurement of Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF), used in treating children suffering from severe acute malnutrition. He also acknowledged the Kebbi State Government’s contribution of approximately N540 million towards free medical services for children. Juma highlighted UNICEF-supported social health insurance interventions, which he said had expanded healthcare access to approximately 86,000 beneficiaries in Zamfara, 18,000 in Sokoto and 10,000 in Kebbi. In the area of child protection, he said UNICEF had supported the development of child protection legislation, Family Court Rules and social protection policies aimed at strengthening the protection, rehabilitation and reintegration of vulnerable children, including those in conflict with the law. He also highlighted the establishment of a Special Care Baby Unit in Sokoto, with similar interventions being advanced in Kebbi and Zamfara to improve medical attention for premature and low-birth-weight babies. Despite the interventions, Juma acknowledged that significant challenges remained, particularly the large number of children still excluded from formal education. He said the gap between the 624,000 children identified as out of school and the approximately 68,000 reached through re-enrolment efforts required urgent government intervention, increased funding and stronger community participation. “Identifying these children is only the first step. The real challenge is ensuring that they return to school and remain there to acquire the knowledge and skills necessary for their future,” he said. Addressing concerns over declining international development funding, Juma explained that the financial challenge was a global development issue and not peculiar to Nigeria. He said UNICEF was intensifying its resource mobilisation strategies to sustain critical interventions and support state governments, assuring that education programmes across the three states had not been affected by the funding decline experienced earlier in the year. On the difficulties of delivering services in remote and insecurity-affected communities, he said UNICEF was working through government structures, field facilitators and third-party monitoring arrangements to ensure that interventions reached vulnerable children and women. He called for stronger coordination at ward and local government levels, stressing that protecting children’s rights was a collective responsibility that should not be left to UNICEF or government institutions alone. “We need the active participation of government agencies, development partners, civil society organisations, traditional and religious leaders, community structures and parents. Journalists must also use their platforms to educate communities, generate demand for essential services and hold stakeholders accountable for their commitments to children,” he said. As part of efforts to strengthen media participation, Juma invited journalists to join future field visits to document UNICEF-supported projects and independently assess their impact on vulnerable communities. He also urged media organisations across the three states to support the December 5 to 11, 2026 polio immunisation campaign through public awareness, pre-campaign mobilisation and community engagement to encourage parents and caregivers to present eligible children for vaccination. The briefing concluded with a renewed call for collective action as the world marks the 2026 World Children’s Day under the theme, “My Day. My Rights. My Future.” UNICEF maintained that protecting children’s rights must go beyond policy declarations and public commitments to sustained investment, effective service delivery and measurable accountability, warning that the future of the region depended largely on the commitment of its leaders and communities to protect, educate and empower the next generation. items.title: Crise de Ceuta : le rapport qui enfonce le Maroc
items.description: Et si l’assaut massif de migrants, fin juillet dernier, sur l’enclave espagnole de Ceuta avait été orchestré par le Makhzen ? C’est en tout cas la piste que suggère un rapport, d’abord classifié puis déclassifié, du Cenif (Centre national de l’immigration et des frontières de la police espagnole), cité de nouveau il y a quelques jours dans un long reportage de l’émission « Envoyé spécial », diffusée sur France 2. Crise de Ceuta : des preuves sur l’implication du Maroc Bien évidemment, le rapport ne désigne pas nommément le Maroc comme étant l’instigateur de cet assaut spectaculaire, qui a provoqué une crise politique en Espagne et des remous dans toute l’Europe. Mais il documente un faisceau d’éléments troublants laissant penser à une action coordonnée par le « Maroc profond ». Professeur à l’université de Ceuta, Enrique Perez Avila, interrogé dans le reportage, est formel : « Il est presque impossible de faire se déplacer 80.000 personnes en 24 heures qui n’ont rien de commun. C’est le Maroc qui a orchestré l’entrée massive. » Dans son rapport, la police espagnole relève que, quelques jours avant la traversée, des messages incitant à passer la frontière et contenant des instructions ont envahi la Toile et des groupes privés sur WhatsApp, de manière automatisée et coordonnée. « Tous ces groupes agissent de la même manière et en même temps », soutient Enrique Perez Avila. « Il n’est pas concevable que ce soit spontané. » « Le 30 juillet 2026, nous allons lancer une attaque contre Ceuta », indiquait l’un de ces messages. « Il ne dit pas : nous allons émigrer, mais nous allons attaquer », observe le professeur. Autre message : « Les amis, il faut avancer par groupes de dix. Joignez-vous à ce groupe pour coordonner un assaut collectif. Prenez le train pour Tanger, puis le taxi et marchez pendant une heure et demie jusqu’à Fnideq », du nom d’une ville située à environ 30 km au Nord de Tétouan et à quelques kilomètres seulement au Sud de Ceuta. « Il s’agit d’instructions très précises. C’est une campagne pour dire : “Allez-y”, mais aussi pour expliquer comment faire », relève Enrique Perez Avila. L’attitude étrange des policiers marocains Le rapport documente également l’attitude permissive et suspecte des forces de l’ordre face aux flots incessants de migrants. Sur l’une des images, le reportage montre deux agents en uniforme adossés à un muret et regardant passivement le spectacle qui se déroule sous leurs yeux. Une autre image montre également des agents postés le long d’une route, observant impassiblement un camion bondé de jeunes, sans visiblement chercher à l’arrêter. « S’agit-il de policiers démunis face à l’ampleur du mouvement de foule ou ont-ils pour instruction de ne pas intervenir ? », s’interroge l’auteur du reportage. Mais le plus compromettant pour les autorités marocaines, qui, dès l’éclatement de la crise, s’en sont lavé les mains et ont nié toute implication, réside dans la présence, comme le montrent de nombreuses images consignées dans le rapport de la police espagnole, d’individus en civil au « comportement étrange » au cœur de la foule. « Ce rapport décrit l’attitude de ces personnes en civil qui semblent faire preuve d’autorité sur les migrants. Cette personne n’est pas en train de courir vers la frontière, elle semble surveiller. C’est le cas de celui-ci et de celui-là, et certains semblent donner des instructions. Qui sont ces gens ? », se demande le professeur, en passant sous la loupe et en analysant les photographies qui défilent sous ses yeux. Selon le reportage, le rapport révèle l’existence d’images montrant ces hommes en civil donnant des indications aux migrants, et même aux forces de l’ordre, donnant ainsi l’impression de gérer les flux, freinant les uns et incitant les autres à avancer, à proximité de la plage frontalière. « Je ne suis pas en mesure d’affirmer qu’il s’agit des services secrets. D’ailleurs, le Maroc dit qu’il n’y a pas de preuves que les autorités marocaines aient participé. Il faut donc voir à quel niveau d’autorité ils appartiennent, car quelqu’un a bien dû leur donner un ordre », soutient le professeur. L’Espagne va-t-elle finir par accuser le Maroc ? Faute de disposer de preuves permettant d’identifier le donneur d’ordre, la police espagnole s’est gardée d’accuser directement le Maroc. Objet d’une enquête judiciaire toujours en cours, les événements de Ceuta, quand bien même l’Espagne officielle a jusqu’ici exonéré le Royaume pour d’évidentes considérations géopolitiques et économiques, pourraient bien finir, à la lumière de ce rapport accablant de la police, par dévoiler la nature perfide du Makhzen. Un système qui, de l’avis de nombreux spécialistes, a toujours utilisé la question migratoire comme levier pour faire pression sur l’Espagne et, au-delà, sur l’Europe. Faut-il rappeler que les événements de Ceuta ont curieusement éclaté au lendemain de la visite de Pedro Sánchez à Alger ? Ils sont également intervenus dans un contexte où Israël était au banc des accusés pour son génocide à Gaza, dont l’Espagne a été l’un des pays les plus virulents à dénoncer les responsables. items.title: Un passé plus beau que le présent ​
items.description: Pourquoi regrettons-nous parfois ce que nous avions pourtant voulu quitter ? De la séparation amoureuse à la désillusion collective, la nostalgie transforme parfois les expériences douloureuses en souvenirs idéalisés. Mais derrière le désir de retrouver hier se cache peut-être une difficulté plus profonde : celle d’habiter le présent et de se projeter dans l’avenir. Manel Albouchi * Il arrive qu’un patient entre dans le cabinet avec une étrange tristesse. Il parle d’un amour passé, d’une époque qu’il regarde désormais de loin, comme on contemple un paysage depuis la fenêtre d’un train qui ne s’arrête plus. Les souvenirs reprennent leurs couleurs, les conversations retrouvent leur intensité et les moments ordinaires deviennent précieux. ​Et pourtant, hier encore, cette histoire était une cage. ​Il y avait les conflits, les silences, les attentes déçues et ce courage immense qu’il a fallu pour partir. Mais le temps a passé. Ce qui était vécu comme un enfermement s’est progressivement métamorphosé en une époque dorée. ​C’est à se demander comment l’esprit parvient à transformer une expérience douloureuse en un objet de désir. ​La mémoire n’est pas une photographie fidèle du passé. Elle sélectionne, filtre, réorganise. Les blessures perdent parfois de leur intensité, tandis que les instants heureux acquièrent une valeur nouvelle. Nous ne regrettons donc pas toujours ce que nous avons vécu. Nous regrettons parfois ce que nous étions, la place que nous occupions ou les possibilités que nous avions imaginées. ​Au fond, il arrive que nous ne pleurions pas seulement l’autre, mais la personne que nous étions à ses côtés. ​L’art subtil d’arranger les souvenirs ​C’est fascinant de voir ce même mécanisme à l’œuvre à une autre échelle : les peuples peuvent eux aussi éprouver cette étrange nostalgie de ce qu’ils ont un jour voulu quitter. Mais comment ? ​Le passé possède un avantage singulier : nous en connaissons déjà la fin. Il est devenu un territoire familier, dont les contours semblent plus lisibles que ceux d’un présent traversé par l’incertitude. Le présent s’impose avec ses contraintes, ses factures et ses inquiétudes ; le passé, lui, peut être réorganisé par le souvenir. ​Cette reconstruction n’est pas nécessairement une falsification consciente. Elle participe de notre manière de donner une continuité à notre histoire. Mais elle peut aussi produire une idéalisation : les expériences contradictoires s’effacent progressivement au profit d’un récit plus rassurant. ​Comme l’a montré le sociologue Maurice Halbwachs, la mémoire n’est jamais un phénomène purement individuel, car nos souvenirs s’inscrivent toujours dans des cadres sociaux qui les structurent. Nous nous souvenons à travers les groupes auxquels nous appartenons et les récits que nous partageons. ​Ainsi, la nostalgie peut devenir une manière collective de reconstruire le passé. ​De quel «avant» parle-t-on vraiment ? ​Quand un peuple se prend à répéter : «Avant, c’était mieux», de quel avant parle-t-il réellement ? ​De la Tunisie des années 70, de celle des années 90 ou de la période précédant 2011 ? ​Pour certains, le passé évoque la stabilité, la sécurité du quotidien et la solidarité de proximité. Pour d’autres, il rappelle la censure, les inégalités, les restrictions et les possibilités confisquées. ​Ces souvenirs ne s’annulent pas les uns les autres. Ils révèlent des expériences sociales différentes d’une même histoire. ​Ce que l’on regrette parfois n’est pas un régime ancien, mais un sentiment de prévisibilité, une forme de cohésion ou la familiarité d’un monde dont les repères semblaient moins fragiles. ​Il faut donc se méfier des nostalgies qui parlent au nom de tous. Une société ne partage jamais un passé parfaitement commun. Elle en conserve des fragments, des blessures et des souvenirs parfois incompatibles. ​La nostalgie collective peut alors devenir un refuge, mais aussi un filtre qui empêche de regarder lucidement ce qui a réellement été vécu. ​Le fantôme des lendemains qui n’ont pas chanté ​Cette complexité s’est intensifiée avec l’onde de choc de 2011, qui a ouvert un horizon d’attente immense. Pendant un temps, l’histoire est redevenue une œuvre possible, portée par le souffle de la dignité, de la liberté et de la justice sociale. ​Mais aux promesses historiques ont succédé les tensions, les difficultés économiques et les désillusions. ​Il existe dès lors une forme de nostalgie particulièrement poignante : celle d’un avenir qui n’a jamais eu lieu. ​On ne pleure pas seulement ce que l’on a perdu, mais ce que l’on a imaginé et que l’on n’a pas réussi à construire. Ce sont les promesses non réalisées, les possibilités interrompues et les trajectoires qui n'ont jamais trouvé les conditions de leur accomplissement. ​Cette nostalgie porte sur un futur devenu souvenir avant même d’avoir existé. ​La jeunesse suspendue entre mémoire et avenir ​Cette interrogation résonne avec une acuité particulière dans le regard de la jeunesse tunisienne. ​Entre précarité professionnelle, chômage, difficultés d’accès à l’autonomie matérielle et sentiment de déclassement, nombre de trajectoires semblent suspendues. Le désir de départ coexiste alors, dans un paradoxe douloureux, avec un attachement profond au pays. ​Certains jeunes regrettent une époque qu’ils n’ont pourtant pas connue. Ils héritent des récits de leurs parents, des souvenirs familiaux et des représentations d’un monde supposément plus solidaire, plus stable ou plus lisible. ​Cette nostalgie par procuration révèle quelque chose d’essentiel : le passé peut devenir un refuge lorsque le présent ne fournit plus suffisamment de prises pour imaginer la suite. ​La nostalgie peut être moins le désir de retourner dans le passé que l’expression d’un présent dans lequel il devient difficile de construire un avenir. ​Derrière le désir de partir se trouve parfois une autre demande : pouvoir vivre dignement, se projeter, devenir autonome et trouver sa place sans devoir renoncer à son appartenance. ​Que pleurons-nous, au fond ? ​Dans une perspective psychanalytique, la perte ne concerne jamais uniquement l’objet que nous avons quitté. Une séparation peut aussi nous faire perdre une place, un projet, une image de nous-mêmes ou une représentation de l'avenir. ​À l’échelle collective, c’est parfois une confiance institutionnelle, une cohésion sociale ou un idéal partagé qui semble disparaître. ​Les générations elles-mêmes se transmettent cette mémoire affective. L’aîné pleure la solidarité de son quartier d’autrefois, l’adulte les promesses de sa jeunesse et le jeune de vingt ans peut nourrir une nostalgie héritée des récits familiaux. ​Mais cette transmission n’est pas neutre. Elle peut préserver une mémoire commune et donner une profondeur à l’appartenance, tout comme elle peut enfermer les nouvelles générations dans un passé qu’elles n’ont pas choisi. ​ Aimer son histoire sans lui vendre son avenir ​Dans son ouvrage The Future of Nostalgia , Svetlana Boym oppose la nostalgie restauratrice, qui vise à reconstruire un passé idéalisé au service d’une identité figée, à la nostalgie réflexive, qui assume la perte irrémédiable du temps par l’ironie et la pensée critique. ​Dans le travail thérapeutique comme dans l’introspection collective, il ne s’agit pas de condamner le regard tourné vers hier, mais de l’écouter. La question peut alors se déplacer : de «Qu’est-ce qui me manque dans le passé ?» vers «Qu’est-ce qui me manque de moi-même ?» et, peut-être, «Qu’est-ce que je peux encore construire ?» ​Une époque a pu être rassurante sans être juste. Une relation a pu être intense sans être salutaire. Une promesse politique a pu être porteuse d’espoir sans avoir trouvé les conditions de sa réalisation. ​Nous pouvons aimer notre histoire, chérir la beauté de ce qui a été, sans pour autant abdiquer face au présent. La maturité d’un individu comme celle d’un peuple consiste peut-être à traverser ses mémoires sans leur déléguer le pouvoir de confisquer l’avenir. * Psychothérapeute. L’article Un passé plus beau que le présent ​ est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Wall Street ends sharply lower on AI selloff, S&P 500, Dow in correction
items.description: US stocks extended their rout on Friday, and the S&P ​500 and the Dow both confirmed corrections after Anthropic’s momentous debut fell flat , exacerbating worries about the AI trade that has driven this year’s stock market rally. All three major US equity ‌indexes ended sharply lower. The Dow and the S&P 500 are now more than 10 per cent below their record closing highs, confirming both indexes have entered a correction. The bellwether S&P 500 notched its seventh consecutive drop, its longest losing streak since February 2020. The S&P 500 and the Dow logged their largest weekly percentage losses since April 2025, when US President Donald Trump announced his market-rattling “ liberation day ” tariff package. The Nasdaq’s weekly drop was its largest since March 2020. The tech-heavy index has dipped into negative ​territory for the year. “This is clearly a challenging day for capital markets, and as we head into a Friday close, it appears to be accelerating to a certain ​degree,” said Bill Northey, senior investment director at US Bank Wealth Management in Billings, Montana. “But as we step back and evaluate fundamentals and ⁠sentiment, sentiment is clearly winning the day today.” “Sentiment is always the more powerful force in the immediate space, whereas fundamentals tend to win out over time,” Northey added, referring to economic ​strength and solid corporate earnings, among other things. Anthropic’s supersized debut as a publicly held company, which was intended to raise as much as $2 trillion in market cap, failed to catch ​fire on Thursday, closing 17.1pc above its $83 offer price as enthusiasm for the stock faded throughout the session. In its second day as a publicly held company, Anthropic’s shares fell 9.1pc; Nvidia’s shares tumbled 13.8pc. The Anthropic IPO , combined with Nvidia’s quarterly earnings report, failed to dispel fears over risks associated with artificial intelligence and the massive expenditures on the nascent technology. “Nvidia reported what might have been one of the greatest quarters in corporate ​earnings history; they did everything right,” said Chuck Carlson, chief executive officer at Horizon Investment Services in Hammond, Indiana. “A lot of people, myself included, were looking to the Anthropic debut to ​some extent as a clearing event, and it wasn’t.” The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index, which has powered much of the broader stock market’s gains in recent months, was up as much as 106.6pc in ‌mid-June. That ⁠lustre has faded, with the index’s year-to-date advance having shrunk to 18.7pc. Among hyperscalers, Amazon fell 3.9pc, while Meta dropped 5.9pc. Neocloud firm CoreWeave fell 12.1pc and its peer Nebius slid 16.1pc. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 949.73 points, or 1.93pc, to 48,147.33; the S&P 50 lost 265.41 points, or 3.70pc, to 6,910.42 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 1,261.47 points, or 5.28pc, to 22,617.73. The CBOE Market Volatility Index, often referred to as Wall Street’s “fear gauge,” rose to its highest close since April 7, 2025.

items.title: Les lauréates des Prix Besrour d’excellence en médecine
items.description: Le 20 novembre 2026, la Faculté de médecine de Sousse a accueilli la cérémonie des Prix Besrour d’excellence en médecine et sciences de la santé. Co-organisée par les quatre facultés de médecine de Tunisie et la Faculté de médecine de l’Université de Montréal, avec l’appui de la Fondation Dr Sadok Besrour, cette cérémonie est devenue un rendez-vous de référence pour la communauté médicale universitaire. Il s’agit de reconnaître l’excellence, inspirer la relève médicale tunisienne . Cette édition marque une étape nouvelle : pour la première fois, le Dr Sadok Besrour a décerné un Prix de la meilleure thèse de doctorat en médecine dans chacune des quatre facultés, à Tunis, Sousse, Monastir et Sfax. Reconnaître la qualité de la recherche dès le doctorat, c’est encourager une culture scientifique durable au cœur de la formation médicale. Les lauréates de cette session sont: Prix d’excellence en pédagogie : Pr Ag Nadia Ghariani, Faculté de médecine de Sousse. Prix d’excellence en recherche : Pr Ag Wala Ben Kridis, Faculté de médecine de Sfax. Prix de la meilleure thèse : Dr Ahlem Radaoui, Faculté de médecine de Tunis. Dr Mraiam Maaref, Faculté de médecine de Sousse Dr Wissal Khalil, Faculté de médecine de Monastir Dr Oumayma Elleuch, Faculté de médecine de Sfax La matinée a également donné lieu à deux conférences tournées vers l’avenir de l’enseignement : l’intelligence artificielle au service de l’apprentissage en médecine (Pre Latifa Lassouad, Université de Sousse) et les sciences cognitives pour mieux apprendre et mieux enseigner (Dre Catherine Hervouet-Zeiber et Dre Geneviève Benoit, CPASS, Université de Montréal). L’article Les lauréates des Prix Besrour d’excellence en médecine est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: ‘Issakaba Returns’ grosses N47.8m in opening weekend, sets new record for Nollywood action thriller
items.description: By Benjamin Njoku The highly anticipated Nollywood classic, “Issakaba Returns” stormed the domestic box office, recording a spectacular opening weekend gross of N47.8 million to become the highest-grossing debut ever for an action thriller. The film, directed by popular filmmaker and producer, Lancelot Oduwa Imasuen, premiered last Wednesday at Silverbird Cinemas, Victoria Island, Lagos. Celebrating the feat, Lancelot, fondly called D’Guvnor, thanked everyone who showed up, bought tickets, filled the cinemas and embraced “Issakaba Returns” with so much love. “To everyone who has supported this journey, shared the excitement, spread the word and made the opening weekend this remarkable, I do not take your love for granted. “This is more than numbers. It is a testament to the love, nostalgia and connection you all have with this story. “N47.8 million opening weekend gross, and this is only the beginning! “Thank you for believing in us. Thank you for showing up. The love has been organic, and we feel every bit of it,” Lancelot said. The premiere of “Issakaba Returns” was spectacular and memorable. The evening exploded into war songs, cultural dance and gyration as the film began its cinema run. Long before the lights went down inside the cinema hall, the carnival had already begun outside. Drummers, dancers and chanting fans set the mood, recreating the fearless spirit of the Issakaba Boys who, 25 years ago, stood against evil in the South-East. For the lead character, Sam Dede, the return is more than nostalgia. It is a message. Speaking at the premiere, he said the evils the Issakaba Boys fought a quarter of a century ago, kidnapping, money rituals, human trafficking are still ravaging society today. First released in 2001 and inspired by real-life vigilante movements, the original “Issakaba” became a cultural phenomenon. items.title: Yemen’s Houthis launch strikes after Saudi coalition’s 'special operation'
items.description: Yemen’s Houthis launched strikes on the Saudi capital Riyadh on Saturday, after vowing reprisals for a “special operation” by the Saudi-led coalition fighting them. Saudi Arabia has been battling a surge in attacks since fighting reignited in neighbouring Yemen’s civil war this summer, where Riyadh backs the internationally recognised government against the Houthis. An AFP journalist reported hearing two explosions shortly after authorities issued an alert, later lifted, saying the city was “under a hostile aerial threat”. The coalition later said it had “ intercepted and destroyed ” three Houthi ballistic missiles headed for the capital. The Houthis said on that they were striking targets across Saudi Arabia, including in Riyadh. The strikes came after the Houthis vowed revenge for the coalition’s attack on the Red Sea port city of Hodeida and other targets on Friday. The “special operation” hit smuggling and weapons-transporting operations in Hodeida, the coalition said. It also involved attacks on Sanaa, Saada and Taiz governorates, marking an uptick in violence after months of hostilities. The Houthis had vowed to hit the Saudi city of Jeddah and other Red Sea ports if Hodeida was attacked, while warning airlines that Saudi airspace was “unsafe”. The group also threatened Riyadh’s financial district and a power station in Al-Shuqaiq. Meanwhile, Prime minister Shahbaz Sharif strongly condemn the Houthi attack on the King Abdullah Financial District in Riyadh. “Such acts of reckless aggression, targeting civilian infrastructure and economic facilities, are totally unacceptable and threaten regional peace and stability,” he said in a post on X. Pakistan stands in unwavering solidarity with our brotherly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and its people. We fully support the Kingdom’s right to defend its sovereignty and territorial integrity and to protect its citizens and residents, he said. ‘Special operation’ - Coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said its forces had “targeted operational capabilities at Hodeida port that were used in smuggling operations and the transport of weapons and ballistic missiles”. The coalition also hit “military targets” in Sanaa, including missile and drone facilities and a supply depot, he said on X. The Houthis claimed coalition strikes had killed 41 people in the previous 24 hours. Yemen’s Saudi-backed armed forces said dozens of airstrikes and drone attacks, as well as hundreds of artillery attacks, killed or wounded 193 Houthi fighters. These figures were impossible to verify independently. Two ballistic missiles were intercepted over the Jizan region near the Yemen border, the coalition spokesman said, with debris falling in Al-Shuqaiq. The Houthi military spokesman said the group had targeted Al-Shuqaiq power station and Jizan port with “accurate and direct” strikes that caused “extensive damage”. Images of a damaged power station in Mocha after a coalition air raid were broadcast by the Houthis’ Al-Masirah television. The coalition strikes came after a Houthi attack struck a tower in Riyadh’s financial district, the latest high-profile blow against the world’s top oil exporter. Witnesses told AFP that Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper, housing Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund, was damaged. ‘Airspace is unsafe’ - After the coalition warned civilians to evacuate Hodeida port, the Houthis responded by threatening to hit Jeddah and other ports on the Saudi Red Sea coast. The Houthis’ Humanitarian Operations Coordination Centre sent emails to shipping companies and other bodies using Jeddah port, warning them to evacuate. The group warned “all airlines that Saudi airspace is unsafe, as it will be the theatre of our operations in the coming hours, except for the holy airspace over Makkah and Madina”. They also told people to avoid Riyadh’s King Abdullah Financial District, whose offices were evacuated weeks ago, calling it a “military target”. The two sides have exchanged attacks since a four-year truce in Yemen’s civil war collapsed in July. Early on Friday, the Houthis accused the Saudis of striking a civilian boat, killing 19 people. Yemen’s Saudi-backed government forces withdrew from areas near the Red Sea’s Bab al-Mandab strait this month, ceding territory to the Houthis, who launched a sweeping offensive in September. The group has now advanced close to Aden, the interim capital of the internationally recognised government which fled the Houthis’ takeover of Sanaa in 2014. The coalition intervened against the Houthis in early 2015, in a conflict that left hundreds of thousands dead and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. The United Nations expressed concern on Friday over the ongoing attacks.

items.title: Davido and Chioma: The love story continues
items.description: By Benjamin Njoku Afrobeats superstar Davido is known for flaunting his wife, Chioma Adeleke, on social media, displaying public affection and storming international show venues in her company. It is no surprise, therefore, that the three-time Grammy nominee has taken their romance to the studio, borrowing a leaf from the likes of Adekunle Gold and Simi, Banky W and Adesuwa Etomi, as well as Beyoncé and Jay-Z, who have all turned their love stories into music. For Davido, Chioma has never just been his wife. She has been his muse from the very beginning. Their love story in music started in 2018 with ‘Assurance’, the birthday gift Davido dedicated to Chioma when they were still dating. Chioma starred in the video, and the song became one of the most iconic love anthems in Afrobeats history. She returned in 2020 for ‘1 Milli’, whose wedding-themed video further celebrated their relationship. Nearly eight years after ‘Assurance’, ‘Already Falling’ brings that story full circle, from young lovers to husband and wife. The song, the eighth track on Davido’s sixth studio album, “ORIADÉ”, was released on July 31, 2026. It blends English, Yoruba and Nigerian Pidgin, and reimagines Elvis Presley’s timeless classic ‘Can’t Help Falling in Love’ through an Afrobeats lens with background vocals by Peruzz The official video, released on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, stars Chioma as his leading lady once again. Directed by Meji Alabi, who also directed ‘Assurance, the video was filmed at the historic Château de Chanteloup, the estate of French cognac house Maison Martell in Cognac, France. It blends French elegance with Nigerian style, with Davido arriving in a horse-drawn carriage, serenading Chioma in grand interiors, and later recreating a proposal scene by a lake at dusk, where he goes down on one knee to present her with a ring. Though the couple wedded in a lavish Lagos ceremony in June 2024, the proposal scene is a cinematic metaphor for renewed commitment, not a new engagement. Davido announced the release himself with the caption: “Already Falling. From us to you. Enjoy.” Like other music stars, Davido is proving that a real-life love story can become a powerful artistic brand. For fans, ‘Already Falling’ is more than a music video. It is a continuation of a story they have followed since 2018 ; from young lovers, to husband and wife, to parents, told in Davido’s most personal songs. And with Chioma by his side in the studio, on screen, and on tour, including their recent high-profile trip to Tanzania with Diamond Platnumz, the couple shows no signs of slowing down. items.title: Do women control their husbands?
items.description: By Chioma Gabriel, Editor, Special Features It is often said that women are a necessary evil, a desirable calamity and a domestic peril. It all depends on where one is standing. In traditional African societies, a woman’s place was said to be in the kitchen, from where she was expected to work her way into her husband’s heart through his stomach. Women were traditionally expected to be seen but not heard. They were like shadows trailing their husbands, with little or no opportunity to express opinions on matters affecting the family and society. They were often regarded as acquired possessions whose primary responsibilities were to bear children and provide labour on the farms. They had little or no say in the scheme of things. A similar pattern appears in some biblical accounts, where headcounts excluded women and children. When Jesus fed the 5,000 and the 4,000, the recorded figures referred to the men, with women and children excluded from the count. In the early Christian community, Paul’s instruction required women to remain silent in church and ask their husbands questions at home. Although interpretations of this passage differ among Christian scholars, it has historically been cited to support restrictions on women’s public religious participation. Despite these historical and cultural limitations, women have, in different ways, exercised considerable influence over men, including their husbands. Biblical accounts The Bible contains several accounts of women whose actions, decisions or influence significantly shaped the lives of men. Eve persuaded Adam to eat the forbidden fruit after the serpent tempted her in the Garden of Eden. Jezebel manipulated her husband, King Ahab, and orchestrated the murder of Naboth to acquire his vineyard. Delilah used persistent pressure and deception to make Samson reveal the secret of his extraordinary strength. Sapphira conspired with her husband, Ananias, to deceive the apostles about the proceeds from the sale of their property. Michal helped David escape from King Saul but later confronted and despised him over his public dancing before God. Bathsheba, working alongside the prophet Nathan, intervened to ensure that David fulfilled his promise that Solomon would succeed him as king. Sarah persuaded Abraham to have a child through her maidservant, Hagar, and later demanded that Hagar and Ishmael be sent away. Rebekah orchestrated a family deception by persuading her son Jacob to disguise himself as Esau and obtain Isaac’s blessing. Herodias influenced her daughter to demand the head of John the Baptist from her husband, Herod Antipas. Job’s wife, overwhelmed by their suffering, urged her husband to curse God and die. Mary and Martha also demonstrated the emotional influence women could have. When their brother, Lazarus, died, their grief deeply moved Jesus, who wept before raising him from the dead. There is also the account of a woman who anointed Jesus’ feet with her hair, although the biblical accounts differ on the identity of the woman. It is important not to confuse Mary Magdalene with Mary of Bethany or the unnamed woman in Luke’s account. Not all these women controlled their husbands in the strict sense. Some influenced, persuaded, deceived, encouraged or challenged the men in their lives. Nevertheless, their stories demonstrate that women have never been entirely without influence, even in societies structured around male authority. Did Queen Elizabeth 11 control her husband? The marriage between Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip presents an interesting example of a reversal of traditional marital expectations. Elizabeth’s relationship with Philip was largely a partnership shaped by an extraordinary reversal of conventional marital expectations. Philip had to accept that his wife was not only the Queen at home but also his sovereign in public life. When Elizabeth ascended the throne in 1952, Philip suddenly became the husband of a reigning monarch. His position within the royal household changed significantly. He had to accept that his wife outranked him in official protocol. At public ceremonies, he occupied a supporting position, observing the precedence attached to her office. At her coronation in 1953, Philip knelt before Elizabeth and pledged allegiance to her. This was particularly significant because he was her husband, not merely a subordinate royal official. He was not crowned king simply because he was married to the Queen. Instead, he became her royal consort, accompanying her on official engagements and supporting the monarchy. Elizabeth’s position also shaped the royal arrangements surrounding their children and family. In 1957, she formally made Philip a Prince of the United Kingdom, recognising his position within the royal family. However, he did not acquire the constitutional authority of a king. Despite Philip’s strong personality, Elizabeth remained the sovereign and the ultimate constitutional authority. Perhaps the most interesting lesson from their marriage is that a man born into royalty had to spend more than seven decades accepting that his wife occupied a position above his in the constitutional hierarchy. This, however, should not necessarily be interpreted as evidence that Elizabeth controlled Philip in their private relationship. It was primarily a consequence of her position as monarch. Nigerian women who wielded power and influence Nigeria’s history is replete with women who exercised considerable political, economic and traditional authority, even in societies where men dominated public life. Queen Idia of the Benin Kingdom, in present-day Edo State, was the mother of Oba Esigie. She played a significant role in her son’s political and military success. Her influence was so considerable that the position of Iyoba, or Queen Mother, became an important institution in the Benin monarchy. Omu Okwei of Osomari, in present-day Anambra State, was a wealthy businesswoman and influential traditional figure. Her commercial success gave her considerable economic and social authority, extending beyond her household into community affairs. Madam Efunroye Tinubu of Abeokuta and Lagos was a powerful merchant and political figure. She wielded considerable influence in the affairs of Lagos and maintained relationships with powerful traditional rulers. In Ibadan, Iyalode Efunsetan Aniwura was a wealthy trader and powerful female chief whose economic resources gave her considerable political influence. She was not simply a woman operating in her husband’s shadow but an authority in her own right. These women demonstrated that female influence in traditional Nigerian society was not restricted to marriage or domestic relationships. Some wielded power independently through wealth, political connections, traditional institutions and personal achievements. Their stories also challenge the assumption that women have always occupied powerless positions in African societies. However, despite the influence of these historical figures and many contemporary women who hold sway in a male-dominated world, it would be inaccurate to conclude that Nigerian women systematically control their husbands. Different strokes for different folks Every marriage has its own power dynamics. Behind the closed doors of many Nigerian homes, decisions are made, arguments are won and lost, compromises are reached and, sometimes, one partner quietly persuades the other to do things they would ordinarily not have considered. While the husband may traditionally be regarded as the head of the family, it is not unusual to find a wife whose opinion carries considerable weight or whose approval is required before important decisions are taken. In some homes, the man appears to wear the crown, but the woman holds the remote control. This has fuelled an age-old argument: Do women really control their husbands? Is a woman who influences her husband’s decisions exercising wisdom, fulfilling her marital responsibilities or subtly taking over the leadership of the home? Where should the line be drawn between a wife’s influence and outright domination? The debate becomes even more interesting when viewed against the background of biblical teachings, traditional African values and the changing realities of Nigerian marriages, where education, financial independence and evolving gender roles are steadily redefining relationships between husbands and wives. A woman can influence her husband’s decisions without dominating him. She can manage the family finances without becoming a family dictator. She can disagree with her husband without disrespecting him, just as he can exercise leadership without becoming oppressive. Marriage should not be an opportunity for one person to destroy the individuality of another. African traditions, too, contain examples of women whose wisdom, courage and contributions helped sustain powerful families and communities. Perhaps the real question is not who controls the home but who contributes to making it work. A marriage should not be a kingdom where one person reigns while the other lives as a subject. It should be a partnership in which two individuals, with different strengths and perspectives, work towards a common future. The strongest husband is not necessarily the one whose wife never questions him, just as the strongest wife is not the one who always gets her way. The strongest marriage is one in which neither partner needs to dominate the other to feel respected. That, perhaps, is the difference between having a spouse and having a true partner. What people say Taking this topic to the marketplace and engaging ordinary people in conversations about it proved quite interesting. Some respondents looked around, paused and carefully weighed their words before speaking. Clearly, the question of whether women control their husbands touches a sensitive nerve in many marriages. Martina, a married mother of four, said it was not an easy subject to discuss but insisted that every woman exercised some measure of control over her husband. “It is the bad kind of control that is worrisome. For instance, when my elder brother got married, there was something about his wife that put off every member of the family. She was not friendly with us, and one after another, we withdrew and left them alone. “The way my brother, who was very close to us while we were growing up, suddenly stopped caring about us showed that something was wrong. I don’t think it was normal. “He wedded her in the Catholic Church, but shortly afterwards, his wife opened a shrine in the family compound and brought the gods of her own family into ours. Before we knew what was happening, she started calling herself Ezenwanyi. “Our brother, her husband, was her first convert. Before long, he was no longer the brother we knew. He did only what she told him to do, and our family home became a habitat for all manner of native doctors. “Is that not control? We have stopped going home because there is no longer any trust. My brother now behaves like a zombie.” Commenting on his sister-in-law, Kingsley said he had effectively lost his only brother after the latter got married. “We were the only two children of our parents. I am the older one, and we were very close. When I relocated to the United States, I left my apartment and everything in it for my younger brother. I later came home for his wedding and stayed for a while to establish some businesses in Nigeria. I stayed with him. “Because I was based overseas, I decided to use my old Nigerian residential address as my business address. My brother’s wife overheard us discussing the business and its location. She suddenly came out of the bedroom, shouting that her home address must not be used as my business address. “It was the manner in which she spoke to me that baffled me. Ever since then, whenever I speak with my brother, it feels as though I am talking to a stranger. “I am equally married, but my wife continues to maintain cordial relationships with my other relatives. I feel I have completely lost my brother. Anything I ask him now, he would say, let me ask my wife or let me discuss with my wife. He is my only brother and I can no longer confide in him.” For Charles Ezealo, his experience with two marriages exposed the complicated relationship between marital influence and extended family expectations. “I suffered considerable embarrassment after I got married. When I married my first wife, my mother would not allow her to join me in Lagos because she insisted that, having lost our father at a young age and struggled to train her children without assistance, my wife must first ‘marry’ her by coming to stay with her in the village for at least three weeks. “My then wife, who was a medical doctor undergoing her housemanship, refused to accept the arrangement. She eventually divorced me. “My mother subsequently arranged another marriage for me with a village girl from Imo State, whom she had personally selected and approved. She followed me to the UK. “However, things changed when we got there. To cut a long story short, she is not even on speaking terms with my mother and has, on several occasions, opposed her visiting us in the UK. I have never seen anything like it but I think m mother deserved what she got.” For Deacon Fredrick, marriage should be a win-win situation rather than an arrangement in which one partner dominates the other. “Unfortunately, that is not always the case nowadays. I have encountered men who complain that their wives deny them conjugal rights until certain demands are met. Come to the Church, you hear all kinds of things as a marriage counsellor: He snores. She’s too fat. He has body odour. He’s a two-minutes man. All manner of things and people are getting divorced because of these. “Some men also complain that their wives make financial demands beyond their capabilities and use such demands to create tension in their homes. A wise woman should build her home, not destroy it. “But, mind you, not all women control their husbands. Healthy marriages are built on mutual respect, shared decisions and partnership rather than dominance. “Controlling behaviour can occur in any relationship and is not exclusive to one gender. Either a wife or a husband can exhibit controlling tendencies. When a wife attempts to control or micromanage her husband, it may arise from particular relationship dynamics rather than inherent malice.” For 52-year-old Odinaka, a businessman in Lagos, marriage has taught him that being the head of a household does not necessarily mean having the final word on every issue. “I used to believe that whatever I said as the man of the house must stand. But experience has taught me otherwise. My wife understands certain aspects of family life better than I do, particularly finances and the children’s welfare. Sometimes, I may have an idea, but after listening to her arguments, I change my mind,” he said. Although Emeka insists that his wife does not control him, he admits that she has considerable influence over his decisions. His experience reflects a growing reality in many Nigerian households, where women are increasingly participating in decisions traditionally regarded as men’s responsibilities. From choosing where the family lives to deciding how money is spent, determining the children’s education, making investment decisions and managing relationships with extended family members, women are playing increasingly influential roles. For some men, however, this growing influence is interpreted as a threat to traditional masculinity. In a society where many men were raised to believe that authority belongs exclusively to the husband, a wife who questions decisions, insists on being consulted or participates in managing family finances may quickly earn the label of a domineering woman. Yet, some women argue that what men describe as control is often nothing more than participation. “I am not controlling my husband. I simply refuse to be treated like a housemaid in my own home. If we are both contributing financially and raising the children together, why should only one person make decisions?” asked 43-year-old Awele, a civil servant in Lagos. According to her, marriage should not be a military arrangement in which one person gives orders while the other obeys without question. However, not all women exercise influence through open discussions. In some homes, control takes more subtle forms. Some women determine how much money their husbands spend, monitor their movements, influence their friendships and decide which relatives deserve financial assistance. Others use emotional withdrawal, persistent arguments or threats to create pressure until their husbands surrender. Interestingly, some men also exercise similar forms of control over their wives, using financial dependence, intimidation and cultural expectations to enforce obedience. This suggests that the struggle for power in marriage is not exclusive to women. Nigeria’s changing economic realities have also altered traditional household arrangements. With rising living costs, many families depend on the combined earnings of husband and wife to survive. Women who contribute substantially to rent, school fees, feeding and other household expenses increasingly demand a voice in family decisions. However, financial contribution should not become a licence for domination, just as being a husband should not confer unlimited authority. Ultimately, perhaps the more important question is not whether women control their husbands but whether either partner should have absolute control over the other. A successful marriage should not be a competition for supremacy. It should be a partnership in which both individuals can express their opinions, disagree without fear and make decisions without intimidation. items.title: Ensign Global University celebrates its 2026 graduating class in 11th Congregation
items.description: Ensign Global University marked its 11 th Congregation for the 2025/2026 academic year on November 14, graduating 65 Master of Public Health (MPH) students—comprising 32 males and 33 females. The ceremony brought together graduates, families, faculty, staff, and invited guests, including Founder and Board Chair, Dr Lynette Gay and special guest of honour Nene Sakite II, Konor of Manya Krobo and President of the Eastern Regional House of Chiefs, to honour the dedication and resilience that carried the class to this milestone. In his address, the university president, Professor Stephen C. Alder, reiterated Ensign Global’s mission to educate and produce entrepreneurial leaders with high levels of competency and professionalism, generate actionable knowledge to address global challenges, and build mutually beneficial partnerships to advance global public health. He urged graduates to embody the university’s values, become agents of positive change, and use their education to improve the lives of communities and countries worldwide. In his keynote address, Executive Vice President for Health Sciences and CEO of University of Utah Health, Dr Bob S. Carter acknowledged the high level of education and certification the graduates had received and encouraged them to channel the training into serving their communities and spaces. “In 2024, Ensign Global University became the first institution in Africa to earn accreditation from the Council on Education for Public Health (CEPH), the same US body that accredits the schools in Johns Hopkins University… The degree you are receiving today represents a high level of preparation, and now it’s up to you to bring that same commitment to the communities that you serve.” He challenged the graduates to identify gaps in healthcare delivery and create context-appropriate solutions that reflect their communities’ realities and resources, reflecting one of the university’s core pillars. “An idea that is developed somewhere else still has to work right here in our community, in your community, with the people and resources that you have.” Dr Carter further noted the University of Utah’s pride in its partnership with Ensign Global University, describing it as an important collaboration in advancing public health education and practice. Speaking to the graduates, His Majesty Nene Sakite II urged the graduates to measure their impact not by public recognition, but by the lives protected and the communities transformed through their interventions. He added, “When an engineer builds a bridge, everyone can see it. When an architect designs a skyscraper, you can see it. But when the public health professional does their job right, when an outbreak is contained before it spills over, when clean water policies pass before a community gets sick, the reward is an absence.” He remarked that graduates’ education goes beyond academic qualifications. It is a responsibility rooted in justice, human dignity, and promoting healthy living. “You didn’t earn a degree just to put letters behind your name. You earned a license to be stubbornly and relentlessly hopeful in a world that often treats suffering as inevitable.” Blessing Uche graduated as the class’s best graduating student. She and Abraham Gaitu each received a Community Service Award, while Rita Coffie and Pearl Sally Davordzie received the Leadership Awards. Sherif Sulley received the Best Thesis Award for his thesis, “Socioeconomic and Lifestyle Determinants of Hypertension among Adults Aged 18-49 Years in Ghana: A Cross-Sectional Secondary Data Analysis Using the 2014 Ghana Demographic and Health Survey (GDHS).” On Monday, November 10, 2026, Ensign Global University’s flagship project, Health2Go, celebrated a decade of service and impact in Wawase, in the Yilo Krobo Municipality of the Eastern Region. Since 2016, the project has served mothers and children under 5. A study reported by the British Medical Journal last year credited it with a 67% reduction in mortality among children under 5 during the project’s years of service.

items.title: Soludo approves N50,000 December bonus for Anambra workers
items.description: By Vincent Ujumadu Anambra State Governor, Prof. Chukwuma Soludo, has approved a N50,000 December bonus for civil servants in the state, with the payment expected to reflect in their December 2026 salaries. The governor announced the bonus during the 2026 Civil Service Day celebration held at the Jerome Udoji State Secretariat Complex in Awka, where he also approved measures to improve the working environment and productivity of civil servants. Soludo acknowledged the economic challenges facing workers, admitting that their current salaries were inadequate amid prevailing economic conditions. He, however, assured the workers that his administration would only make financial commitments it could realistically fulfil. “I understand the situation and economic conditions, that we need to be able to do something. The pay that we have all over is not enough; I clearly understand it. “But there is one thing I also want to tell you, and that is I don’t play to the wind. Before we get into a commitment, we make sure that it is something that we will always honour,” he said. Addressing comparisons between Anambra’s salary structure and those of other states, the governor urged civil servants to consider the different revenue bases and economic capacities of state governments before making such assessments. He stressed that sustainable governance and responsible financial management, rather than unfulfilled promises, remained the guiding principles of his administration. Soludo also expressed appreciation to the workers for their support during last year’s governorship election, saying he was pleased that public servants overwhelmingly voted for his administration in recognition of its developmental efforts. Responding to three major requests presented by the workers at the event, the governor immediately directed the rehabilitation of roads within the secretariat complex, approved the establishment of an Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Centre and authorised the pruning of overgrown trees across the premises. Earlier, the Anambra State Head of Service, Barr. Ngozi Iwouno, commended Soludo for restoring security and normalcy across the state. She said civil servants could now attend work regularly without fear, noting that the disruption previously caused by Monday sit-at-home orders had been overcome. Iwouno said the improved security situation had restored confidence among workers and enabled them to discharge their duties more consistently. items.title: La Chine vise 100 milliards d’arbres plantés d’ici 2050
items.description: En 1978, face à la progression des déserts du Gobi et du Taklamakan, le pouvoir chinois a lancé le projet de « Grande muraille verte », avec pour objectif de planter 100 milliards d’arbres d’ici 2050. Pékin en est à près des deux tiers, et dans le Nord comme dans le reste du pays, les forêts plantées développent leur couvert végétal 66 % plus rapidement que les forêts naturelles, selon une étude de l’Université de Pékin à Shenzhen Enhanced CO2 response and aging-related dynamics drive a greater leaf area index increase in China's planted forests in comparison to natural forests », Geophysical Research Letters , 2026.'> 1 . Environ les trois quarts de ces forêts plantées se trouvent toutefois au sud de la ligne Qinling-Huai, hors de la zone concernée par la Grande muraille verte, qui n’en abrite qu’un cinquième au maximum 2 . Comme le montre la carte ci-dessous, c’est surtout dans le sud-est du pays que ces plantations occupent la surface la plus importante, la région concentrant environ six forêts plantées sur dix. Au cours du troisième trimestre 2026, les émissions de CO₂ de la Chine ont chuté de 3,1 % sur un an. Cette baisse est toutefois principalement attribuable au recul du charbon dans la production d’électricité et à la baisse de la consommation de pétrole, affectée par la fermeture du détroit d’Ormuz Analysis : China’s quarterly CO2 falls 3 % in largest drop since Covid », CarbonBrief , 6 novembre 2026.'> 3 . Si elles développent plus vite leur couvert végétal et absorbent une quantité importante de CO₂, les forêts plantées comptent souvent peu d’espèces. Dans les régions arides du Nord, des espèces non indigènes comme le peuplier ont tendance à épuiser l’humidité des sols et les réserves d’eau profonde Excessive reliance on afforestation in China’s arid and semi-arid regions : Lessons in ecological restoration », Earth-Science Reviews , 2011.'> 4 . Entre 2000 et 2020, les plantations ont par ailleurs souvent progressé là où des forêts naturelles reculaient, surtout dans le Sud. L’Asie est, aux côtés de l’Europe, l’une des régions qui se sont le plus reboisées depuis 1990. La part de la Chine dans la superficie forestière mondiale a augmenté d’environ 2 points entre 1990 et 2025, tandis qu’elle a reculé de 3 points en Amérique du Sud, notamment en raison de la déforestation de la forêt amazonienne. items.title: BoG’s 300bps rate cut never happened; market rates actually increased – Gideon Boako
items.description: Tano North Member of Parliament, Dr Gideon Boako, has challenged claims that the Bank of Ghana’s reduction of the Monetary Policy Rate from 14% to 11% represents a cut in prevailing market interest rates. He insists that the actual figures show an increase rather than a reduction. In a Facebook post, Dr Boako argued that the widely reported 300-basis-point reduction was hypothetical because the market rate was never at 14% before the latest Monetary Policy Committee announcement. He explained that the market rate stood at 10% in July 2026, increased to 10.50% following a Bank of Ghana transaction on November 9, and subsequently rose to 11% after the Monetary Policy Committee announced its latest decision on November 18. “10% → 11% = +100 basis points (bps) INCREASE. 10.50% → 11% = +50bps INCREASE,” he stated. Dr Boako questioned the basis for celebrating the reported reduction, asking: “Where is your 300bps cut?” He further argued that the adjustment should not be presented as a monetary stimulus to encourage increased credit demand, pointing to the Bank of Ghana’s decision to narrow the interest rate corridor from +/-400 basis points to +/-100 basis points. His comments followed a social media post by Bank of Ghana Governor, Dr Johnson Asiama, who described the reduction in the Monetary Policy Rate from 14% to 11% as a realignment with prevailing market conditions rather than a fresh round of monetary stimulus.

items.title: Mpraeso MP calls for greater Ghanaian ownership of economy under New Economy agenda
items.description: The Member of Parliament for Mpraeso, Davis Ansah Opoku, has called for greater Ghanaian ownership of the country’s economic opportunities, insisting that the government’s New Economy agenda must prioritise indigenous businesses and entrepreneurs. Contributing to the debate on the 2027 Budget Statement, he argued that economic growth projections would have little meaning if ordinary Ghanaians did not experience improvements in their livelihoods. He questioned the significance of the projected 5.2 per cent economic growth in 2027, arguing that the focus should be on how economic policies translate into tangible benefits for citizens. “The economy is of importance, and for me this whole issue about bandying around numbers and telling us that the economy is going to grow by some 5.2% is neither here nor there when it really does not affect the ordinary man on the streets,” he said. Mr Opoku called for a shift from investment policies that rely heavily on foreign participation towards strengthening Ghanaian ownership of productive assets and businesses. “We are Ghanaians, and Ghanaians must begin to own our own wealth,” he declared. On the mining sector, he urged the government to consider competent Ghanaian operators in decisions concerning mining leases, particularly the Tarkwa mining lease, arguing that the country must secure greater economic benefits from its mineral resources. “We need to look for local competent Ghanaians to be able to manage our mines. We need to move beyond the 10% that we always get from our mines,” he stated. He said the same principle should guide the government’s infrastructure, manufacturing and other economic programmes, stressing that Ghanaian contractors and businesses must have meaningful opportunities to participate in projects financed or facilitated by the state. “If you are determined to promote a new economy, a new economy must be owned by Ghanaians and not foreigners,” he told Parliament. Summing up his position, the Mpraeso MP said Ghanaian ownership must be central to the country’s economic transformation. “Our money is ours, our roads are ours, our businesses are ours, and it’s important that we encourage a lot more Ghanaians to be involved in this process,” he said. He maintained that the New Economy agenda would achieve its intended purpose when indigenous businesses were empowered to own productive assets, create jobs and retain a greater share of the value generated within the Ghanaian economy.

items.title: Countries open path towards 'killer robots' pact
items.description: Countries agreed on Saturday to open a path towards finding an international agreement on regulating lethal autonomous weapons systems , though campaigners seeking to stop so-called killer robots were disappointed by the “watered-down” outcome. After five days of gruelling talks at the United Nations, which ran into overtime, states agreed to open the door to building some form of pact over the next two years. However, with warfare undergoing a radical transformation, spurred by artificial intelligence, non-governmental organisations wanted far swifter, legally binding rules on handing power over human life and death to autonomous machines. Talks at the United Nations’ Review Conference of the Convention on Conventional Weapons (CCW) in Geneva stretched well into the early hours of Saturday. The 128 countries party to the CCW “agreed to launch the elaboration of an international instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems, which should be conducted over the next two years”, conference president Julien Thoni told reporters afterwards. The process to get there had been tricky, with countries at odds and full consensus required for any decision. While a majority of states went in favour of a legally binding agreement, countries that have the technology, including the United States and Russia, are reluctant to have their hands tied . The process ahead should flesh out “which weapons can be forbidden according to international humanitarian law, and which is not forbidden but can be regulated”, Thoni told AFP . The Swiss diplomat said some countries had objected to the word negotiate, but had settled on elaborate instead. Campaign groups said the outcome fell well short of expectations. “States adopted a watered-down mandate that fails to chart a clear path towards a legally binding instrument,” said the Stop Killer Robots (SKR) coalition. “Autonomous weapons technology, including AI in the targeting cycle, is being deployed on the battlefield,” said Nicole van Rooijen, SKR’s executive director. “Delaying the creation of a legally binding instrument puts civilians and humanity at risk,” Verity Coyle, the deputy director for arms at Human Rights Watch, branded the outcome “disappointing”. “It does not provide the urgent action needed to agree new rules — but the technology is racing ahead,” she said.

items.title: GSA recovers GH¢400,000 rent arrears after High Court victory
items.description: The Ghana Shippers’ Authority (GSA) has recovered about GH¢400,000 in unpaid rent after securing a High Court ruling that upholds its authority to enforce regulations under the Ghana Shippers’ Authority Act, 2024 (Act 1122). The ruling is expected to strengthen the Authority’s hand in dealing with non-compliance in the shipping and logistics industry as it prepares to step up regulatory enforcement in 2027. Chief Executive Officer of the GSA, Professor Ransford Gyampo, announced the court victory and recovery during a media engagement in Accra on Friday, November 20, 2026. He said the Authority had resorted to garnishee proceedings to retrieve the outstanding rent and was pursuing other legal actions to ensure that its regulatory directives were respected. Prof. Gyampo described the judgment as an important affirmation of the powers conferred on the GSA by Act 1122, which broadened its oversight responsibilities across the shipping and logistics value chain. “The Authority secured a significant High Court ruling affirming the Authority’s enforcement powers under Act 1122, recovered approximately GH¢400,000 in outstanding rent through garnishee proceedings, and pursued further legal action to enforce regulatory directives and promote compliance within the industry,” he said. The 2024 legislation expanded the GSA’s role from trade facilitation and advocacy to include wider regulatory oversight of the commercial activities of shippers and shipping service providers. The law is intended to promote transparency, fairness and efficiency in the sector, while providing the Authority with a stronger legal basis to regulate industry practices and protect the interests of shippers. However, Prof. Gyampo said the full implementation of the law was being held back by delays in finalising the Legislative Instrument (LI) required to provide detailed rules and procedures for its enforcement. He said the LI would offer greater clarity on the regulatory framework and support the effective exercise of the Authority’s expanded mandate. The GSA has consequently placed regulatory oversight, compliance monitoring and shipper protection at the centre of its 2027 agenda. It plans to intensify enforcement activities and pursue breaches of regulatory directives to promote fairer and more transparent commercial dealings throughout the shipping and logistics industry.

items.title: Food suppliers suspend planned picketing over unpaid arrears
items.description: The Controlled Food Suppliers Association has given the Ghana Commodity Exchange (GCX) and the National Food Buffer Stock Company (NAFCO) a reprieve, suspending plans to picket the two institutions over outstanding payments to its members. The decision follows a meeting between the Association’s leadership and the chief executives of NAFCO and GCX on November 19, at which the two institutions appealed for more time to address the payment delays. They proposed that the suppliers suspend their protest to allow for an engagement with the Minister of Education the following week, in a bid to find a solution to the outstanding arrears. In a statement issued on November 20, the Association said it had agreed to the request, expressing the expectation that the planned ministerial meeting would help resolve the matter. The arrangement also provides for a further meeting between the Association’s leadership and the relevant stakeholders after the engagement with the Minister. The Association said its executives would be invited to that meeting to discuss the outcome of the consultations and the way forward. The suspension of the picketing is therefore tied to the proposed engagements, as suppliers await action to settle the payments owed to them.

items.title: Black Challenge make history with Turkey win to set up Amputee World Cup final against Morocco
items.description: Ghana’s Black Challenge have reached the final of the 2026 Amputee Football World Cup for the first time in their history after beating defending champions Turkey 4-2 on penalties in the early hours of Saturday in Mexico. The semi-final encounter ended 1-1 after extra time, with Ghana holding their nerve in the shootout to secure a historic victory. Star forward Mubarik Mohammed broke the deadlock with a penalty in the first half of extra time, taking his tournament tally to seven goals. However, Turkey responded shortly afterwards to restore parity and force the contest into a penalty shootout. Both teams were reduced to six players following red cards, but the Black Challenge held their composure to book their place in the final. Ghana will face Morocco on Monday at 1:30 am in a bid to win their first-ever Amputee Football World Cup title.

items.title: Mpraeso MP challenges Big Push figures in 2027 Budget
items.description: The Member of Parliament for Mpraeso, Davis Ansah Opoku, has questioned was he said were discrepancies in the financial allocations for the government’s Big Push infrastructure programme, demanding clarity on the actual amount Parliament is being asked to approve. Contributing to the debate on the 2027 Budget Statement, the MP pointed to figures contained in paragraphs 1552 and 1629, as well as Appendix 3C, which he said did not appear to match. He argued that the differences raised questions about the accuracy of the programme’s financial details and Parliament’s ability to properly scrutinise the proposed expenditure. “These are three different figures for the same programme in a budget. So which one are we approving?” he asked. Mr Opoku said government must provide a consistent account of its financial commitments to enable Parliament to exercise its constitutional responsibility of approving public spending. He also raised concerns about the procurement arrangements for the proposed 198.7-kilometre Accra–Kumasi Expressway, drawing attention to paragraph 922 of the Budget Statement, which refers to international competitive tendering for the project. The MP argued that despite government indicating that substantial financing was available for the infrastructure programme, the procurement approach could leave Ghanaian contractors competing against foreign firms for major projects. “Instead of giving it to local contractors, you are now going to bring foreigners from China and elsewhere to come and bid for this work at the detriment of a local contractor,” he stated. He maintained that the benefits of infrastructure spending should extend beyond road construction to include opportunities for local businesses, contractors and workers. “If you are determined to promote a new economy, a new economy must be owned by Ghanaians and not foreigners,” he declared. Mr Opoku called for transparency in the presentation of the Big Push allocations and procurement processes that allow indigenous contractors to compete meaningfully for major public infrastructure projects.

items.title: Cummins wins Cricket Australia's 'unanimous support' to remain Test captain
items.description: Cricket Australia threw its “unanimous support” behind Pat Cummins to remain Test captain Saturday, rejecting any suggestion his integrity had been compromised by the lingering “Sandpapergate” scandal. Cummins has been under huge pressure since Usman Khawaja claimed the whole team knew about the plot to alter the ball in a Test at Cape Town in 2018. He strenuously denied being aware of what was going on in a press conference last week, but his position was undermined when Cameron Bancroft backed Khawaja’s version of events. Only then-captain Steve Smith, his deputy David Warner and Bancroft – who used the sandpaper – were found to be responsible by a Cricket Australia probe. With speculation over Cummins’ future rampant and a home four-Test series against New Zealand next month, CA moved to stamp out any further discussion about the 33-year-old’s fate after meeting him to check on his welfare. It came after Josh Hazlewood earlier Saturday suggested he could quit if any action was taken against his long-time bowling partner. CA expressed “its unanimous support for Pat Cummins as captain” following a board meeting. “We are absolutely determined to steward Australian cricket through this very difficult time with diligence and patience and to listen and learn,” said chairman David Boon. “We’ve expressed our support to Pat and our concern for everyone impacted by the events of the 2018 tour of South Africa. “We have learned from that experience and are proud of the team and the culture Pat and other leaders in the team have fostered over the past eight years and unequivocally reject any implication that Pat’s integrity has been compromised.” The retired Khawaja reignited the controversy in his autobiography, alleging the whole team was in the know, and he was strongly backed by close friend Warner. After Cummins’ denials, Bancroft dropped a bomb in a newspaper column by also claiming “it was the whole team” while saying he felt “angry and betrayed” by the Test skipper. Cricket Australia has ruled out reopening its investigation but instead set up a forum for players to share their experiences about 2018. Great leader Cummins said being captain “carries with it an awesome responsibility. I have and never will take that lightly”. “David and Todd (Greenberg) have a very tough job navigating cricket through all of this and I commend them for reaching out to me and to many of the players and staff from 2018,” he added. “I support the forum 100 per cent. I will be there. All of the players and staff I have spoken with are very keen to go and to have their say. “There will be a lot of difficult conversations but that is what’s needed. Otherwise, from this point, captaining the Australian team in Perth (at the first Test) will be my focus and priority.” Hazlewood threw his support behind Cummins earlier Saturday and made a veiled threat to call it a day if he was removed as captain. He reiterated that the bowling group at the time, which also included Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon, were not part of the plan. They jointly released a statement in 2021 denying any involvement. “I want to back Pat and everything he said in his press conference last week, everything he’s done for the last five or six years in particular as captain,” Hazlewood told the Sydney Daily Telegraph in his first comments since the story blew up. “He’s a great leader. If you went around and asked everyone in the team, you’d hear the same response.” Asked if he would consider quitting in protest if Cummins was removed, Hazlewood said: “I think I’d have to be put in that position to make a decision, but you’d have to think about it, yeah.” Starc has also reinforced that he knew nothing in recent days. Lyon and Smith have yet to comment.
